paras: The lynching of Allen Small was the killing of a Black prisoner by a mob of about 25 men who broke into the Moore County jail at Lynchburg, Tennessee, on the night of September 24, 1903. Small, charged with an attempted assault on a white woman, had been moved to Nashville in August after a judge warned he would be lynched at Lynchburg. A coroner's jury named 27 men and a grand jury indicted 22, which wire reports called probably the first indictment of white lynchers in the South; four defendants were acquitted in October 1904.

On August 12, 1903, Deputy Sheriff Dwyer arrested Small near Tullahoma on a charge of attempting to assault Mrs. Eliza M. Eggleston at her Moore County home. Circuit Judge Higgins said Small would be lynched if carried to Lynchburg and ordered him sent to the Nashville jail, where he was placed the next morning "to escape a band of determined citizens of Moore county." According to a later Chattanooga dispatch, he was returned to Lynchburg on assurances that the danger had passed, and at his preliminary hearing the warrant was reduced to simple assault after Mrs. Eggleston said she could not identify her assailant.

Shortly before midnight on September 24, about 25 men demanded the keys to Small's cell from the sheriff, who was alone and refused. In the Lynchburg account sent to the Nashville Banner, the sheriff fired and wounded one man, but even after two policemen and several citizens arrived, the mob battered down two doors, entered the cell and put a rope around Small's neck. Finding they could not take him out to hang him, the men shot him in the jail.
The sheriff and his guard held three of the fleeing men, Dock Hasty, John Hasty and John Dean, and the Columbia Herald said the mob came mostly from Moore County districts and Tullahoma.

While the coroner's jury sat, deputies found suspect Joe Willis Tanksley with a leg wound his friends blamed on a mule, though his doctor produced a bullet. On September 29 the jury found Small "deliberately, maliciously and premeditatedly" murdered and named 27 men; fourteen were under arrest and three who turned state's evidence were released on bond.

On October 9 the Moore County grand jury was reported to have indicted 22 men for second-degree murder, and the cases were put over to the February term. In October 1904 a jury acquitted Ike Cobb, Dock Hastick, Joseph Toursley and James F. Hastick; the Evening Star headed this "More Alleged Lynchers Acquitted," but no earlier verdict or conviction appears in the coverage.

The August threat appeared only in brief white Tennessee and Kentucky dispatches that called the would-be lynchers "determined citizens." The killing went out on the wires under headlines about the fight at the jail, such as the New York Evening World's "Mob Fought to Kill a Prisoner," with praise for the sheriff's "stout resistance." The coroner's verdict ran widely, headed "Killed by Mob in Cold Blood" in the Bisbee Daily Review, and one version stressed that this was probably the first indictment of white men in the South for lynching. Nearer home, the Columbia Herald called the attackers "His Murderers" and doubted the mule story.

Black weeklies took up the case at the inquest, reprinting the verdict wire under headlines such as "Arrest Southern Lynchers" (Wisconsin Weekly Advocate) and "Southern White Men Held for a Lynching" (Iowa Bystander). In December the Los Angeles Liberator, in an editorial titled "Lynchers May Be Lynched," hoped "the whole gang" would be punished and argued that "the man who will murder a negro will murder a white man." No Black-press report of the August threat, the killing itself or the acquittals appears in the coverage.

A Chattanooga dispatch differed from the Banner account, crediting City Marshal Parks with opening fire and saying the mob beat Small with gun butts and riddled him with bullets, after which he lived about an hour. The sheriff is named Davidson in the wire reports and Stephenson or Stevenson in Tennessee and Chattanooga reports. The Chattanooga dispatch also assigned the 27 names to a grand jury, while a later Nashville dispatch gave the grand jury's figure as 22.

reader.title: Lynching of Allen Small
bases: A mob of about 25 men broke into the Moore County jail at Lynchburg and shot Allen Small, a Black prisoner awaiting the grand jury, after a threatened lynching in August had led officials to move him to Nashville (A1, A2, A4, A5).

Small was shot dead in the jail by a mob of about 25 that overpowered the sheriff (A4, A5); he was held on a charge of assaulting a white woman (A8, A14), and a coroner's jury called the killing deliberate murder (A9).

The Banner special (A5), the wire (A4), the local Columbia Herald (A12, A13) and a Chattanooga dispatch (A14) agree that a mob broke into the Lynchburg jail and killed Small, though they differ on details.

accounts.gist: The sheriff, alone, refused the keys and wounded a mob member; the mob broke two doors, roped Small, and, unable to take him out, shot him dead in the corridor; three were captured.

accounts.label: Chattanooga dispatch (history of the case)
accounts.gist: City Marshal Parks opened fire and officers fired until out of ammunition; the mob beat Small with gun butts and riddled him with bullets, and he lived about an hour.

accounts.label: Local Tennessee paper
accounts.gist: The Columbia Herald named the three captured men, placed the mob's origin in Moore County districts and Tullahoma, and followed the coroner's inquiry and wounded suspects.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Small was deliberately, maliciously and premeditatedly murdered; 27 men named.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: The Liberator welcomed the indictment of fourteen and argued that law enforcement was the South's only hope.

framing.detail: August dispatches called the would-be lynchers 'a band of determined citizens' and reported the transfer as safekeeping ('Taken to Nashville for Safe Keeping').
Wire headlines stressed the battle at the jail ('Mob Fought to Kill a Prisoner', 'With Bullets Negro's Body Riddled by Mob in Jail') and the sheriff's 'stout resistance.'
Some verdict-wire headlines condemned the killing ('Killed by Mob in Cold Blood') or stressed the novelty of indicting white lynchers.
The local Columbia Herald headed its reports 'Three of His Murderers Are Captured' and 'Probing for Murderers' and doubted the suspect's 'mule story.'
Black weeklies ran the coroner's-verdict wire under headlines such as 'Arrest Southern Lynchers' and 'Southern White Men Held for a Lynching.'
The Liberator editorial 'Lynchers May Be Lynched' called the indicted men 'murderers' and hoped 'the whole gang' would be punished.
